data.name: BLEAK: Welcome to Glimmer
data.detailed_description:
Having spent his life locked inside, protected by his sister, and hidden from an extremely hostile world, a young Sourcer named “Bleak” passed the time using his creativity and ingenuity to rebuild a destroyed C.O.G. surveyor robot name "Glitch". When his sister, Asha is discovered and arrested, Bleak emerges with Glitch by his side into this unfamiliar and overwhelming terrain. Can you traverse it?

Welcome to Glimmer

  • 20+ Platforming levels (Multiple ways of beating levels that change the path you take)
  • Competitive Time Trial Online Leaderboards
  • Two playable characters with unique mechanics
  • A massive lore that spans thousands of years across seven original races
  • Strong focus on single-player narrative story telling
  • 20+ original songs

Escape from Wither (est. Late 2024 w/ Remaster):

  • Additional 20+ Platforming levels (Multiple ways of beating levels that change the path you take)
  • Another playable character
  • Lore expansion with greater details on the origin of Pinnacle
  • Strong focus on single-player narrative storytelling.
  • Additional 15+ original songs

reviews.review:
BLEAK: Welcome to Glimmer is a difficult 2D platformer that caught my attention because it has a much bigger world behind it than I expected. I play as Bleak, a young Sourcer who has spent most of his life hidden away with his sister Asha. After she is discovered and arrested, Bleak finally leaves his home with his rebuilt robot Glitch and has to make his way through Glimmer. The game is built around platforming first, but there is also a proper story and a huge amount of lore about the world, its races and its history. It feels like the first part of something much bigger rather than a completely self contained adventure.

The platforming is definitely the part I spend most of my time dealing with. There are more than 20 levels, and the game is very clear about wanting to make me work for every bit of progress. Some levels have multiple routes, so I can sometimes choose a safer path or try something more difficult if I want a better time. I like that because the challenge is not just about reaching the end. Once I understand a level, I can start looking for faster routes and trying to improve how I move through it. The time trial leaderboards give that side of the game some extra purpose too.

The difficulty is where I have the most mixed feelings. BLEAK is deliberately very hard, and there are plenty of sections where I have to repeat the same part several times before I finally get the timing right. I do enjoy that kind of challenge when I can see exactly what I did wrong, but there are moments where the difficulty starts feeling more frustrating than rewarding. Some of the movement mechanics, especially sections involving ropes and tricky platforming, take a while to get comfortable with. The developers did patch several early problems with things like rope collisions, enemy behaviour and level collision, but the game still has some rough edges that I have to accept.

What surprised me most is how much effort has gone into the world and soundtrack. The story covers thousands of years of history and seven original races, while the game has more than 20 original songs. I do not need to understand every piece of the lore to enjoy the platforming, but it gives the game a stronger identity than a basic collection of difficult levels. I also like having two playable characters with different mechanics because it gives the gameplay a little more variety. The darker setting and strange futuristic world fit the title really well.

The main thing holding it back for me is that it can sometimes feel like I am playing the first part of a much larger game rather than getting a complete experience. This is specifically Act One, and the story is clearly setting up a bigger world and continuation. That is fine if I am interested in the lore, but it also means some of the story does not feel completely resolved. I also think the presentation has aged a little since the original release in 2016. The ideas are interesting, but some animations and visual details are not as polished as I would expect from a newer platformer. There is a remastered version that expands the experience considerably, but I am judging this original release on what it actually provides.

I do like that the original game is completely free. That makes a big difference to me because I am getting more than 20 levels, two playable characters, the story, achievements, time trials and a large soundtrack without having to pay for the base game. There are also 30 achievements, which gives me another reason to go back and try to master levels rather than simply finishing them once. I think the game works best when I treat the difficulty as the main challenge and accept that I am going to fail quite a lot before I get better at the movement.

Overall, BLEAK: Welcome to Glimmer is a solid little platformer with more ambition than I expected. I like the difficult level design, multiple routes, different characters, strong soundtrack and surprisingly large amount of lore. The rougher presentation, frustrating moments and unfinished feeling of the Act One story stop it from reaching the really high scores I give to my favourite platformers, but the free price makes the package much easier to appreciate. For me, it is a game with a good amount of personality that does not always get everything right, but there is enough here to make Glimmer worth exploring.

Rating: 7.6/10
